speaker: John Quinn
title: Ep 110 | John B. Quinn | Big Law Litigation Trailblazer & Pioneer
question: In commercial law, what makes a strictly litigation-only firm such a powerful business model compared to full-service firms?
guest: I can't say there was ever a point where we made that conscious decision. The fact is, when we started the firm there were four of us, and we were all litigators. Our strategy was to do whatever it takes to get hired, impress the client, and get hired again and again. It was successful, so we started to grow, we were known as litigators, and other clients came. There just came a point where we realized this was a very powerful business model. We're not trying to be all things to all people—like we're super in tax, super in M&A, capital markets, and all these different areas. It was just this very simple message to the business and legal community: we do one thing, we do disputes work, and we're really good at that.

points.core: Full-service firms dilute credibility by claiming excellence across every practice area.
points.note: Accept: trying to be all things to all people across tax, M&A, or capital markets weakens a firm's perceived mastery in disputes. Do not credit: generic claims that full-service firms are merely too large or bureaucratic.

points.core: Focusing exclusively on disputes sends one clear positioning message to clients.
points.note: Accept: a single-practice disputes identity makes the firm's core expertise immediately legible to the business and legal market. Do not credit: vague praise of specialization without tying it to market messaging or client perception.

points.core: Strong execution on initial matters drives compounding repeat engagements from clients.
points.note: Accept: impressing clients on an early engagement generates recurring litigation work and organic growth. Do not credit: generic platitudes about doing good work or providing good customer service.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core advantage is freedom from conflicts. A full-service firm earns steady fees from banks, private equity houses and large corporates on transactional and advisory work, so it cannot (or will not) sue those same institutions. A litigation-only firm has no such relationships to protect, which lets it act against the biggest defendants and take on the most lucrative disputes that conflicted firms must turn away. It also becomes a natural recipient of referrals from full-service firms, who can send conflicted matters without fear of losing the client's corporate work.

Several other strengths follow from that. Specialisation builds a trial-ready reputation and deep bench that attracts bet-the-company cases and top advocates. Without lower-margin practice areas to subsidise, profitability per partner tends to be very high; Quinn Emanuel and Wachtell-style focus models illustrate this. Independence also allows flexible pricing: contingency fees, damages-based agreements and partnerships with litigation funders, giving the firm upside in claimant work that hourly-billing firms rarely capture. Finally, disputes are counter-cyclical, so revenue holds up or rises in downturns.

The trade-off is lumpier income and no cross-selling from a transactional client base.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
A strictly litigation-only firm derives its greatest commercial advantage from freedom from conflicts of interest. Full-service firms rely heavily on recurring transactional, regulatory, and advisory work from major banks, private equity funds, and large corporations, which ethically or commercially bars them from suing those institutions or arguing adverse legal positions. Litigation boutiques have no corporate retainer relationships to protect, enabling them to sue almost any counterparty and capture high-stakes, plaintiff-side commercial claims that full-service competitors must decline.

This focus also turns full-service rivals into reliable referral sources: transactional powerhouses gladly send conflicted-out disputes to a pure litigation shop, confident it will never poach their deal or advisory business. Moreover, unencumbered by institutional client pressure or rigid hourly-billing cultures, litigation-only firms freely embrace contingency, hybrid, and success-fee arrangements that align client incentives and generate outsized returns. Finally, because every hiring decision and resource centers on courtroom advocacy rather than servicing deal pipelines, these firms maintain leaner overhead, enjoy counter-cyclical resilience when dealmaking slows, and project genuine trial-readiness that commands superior verdicts and settlements.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A litigation-only firm can be very strong, but it isn't better than a full-service firm by default. Its advantages come from a few specific features.

The biggest is fewer conflicts. Because it has no corporate, banking or M&A practice tied to large institutions, it is far less likely to be conflicted out. That lets it sue major banks, tech companies or insurers that full-service firms often can't take on. Quinn Emanuel built much of its brand this way. Focus also builds expertise and reputation: every partner develops trial skills, and some corporate clients hire these firms precisely because they don't compete for their transactional work. The model is also lean. Fewer practice groups to subsidise and lower overhead can support high profits per partner, and many of these firms are comfortable with contingency or success fees, as Susman Godfrey and Bartlit Beck are.

The trade-offs are real. Revenue is lumpy and depends on big cases. There's no steady advisory work feeding new disputes, and the firm can't sell clients a one-stop relationship. Full-service firms make up for this with diversified income that holds up across economic cycles.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
A strictly litigation-only firm’s greatest structural advantage is freedom from conflicts of interest. Full-service firms depend on recurring corporate, finance, and regulatory work from major banks, insurers, and large corporations, which prevents them—both ethically and commercially—from suing those institutions. Because a litigation boutique does not maintain those ongoing transactional relationships, it can freely take adverse positions against the world’s largest companies, capturing high-stakes plaintiff and defense work that full-service firms must turn away.

This model also turns competitors into referral sources. Full-service firms regularly send conflicted disputes to litigation-only boutiques because they know the boutique will not try to poach the client’s lucrative corporate or M&A work. Financially, pure litigators avoid the overhead and cyclicality of large transactional practices and can more easily adopt contingency or hybrid fee arrangements with massive upside. Finally, singular focus on disputes fosters genuine trial readiness, giving these firms superior courtroom credibility and stronger leverage in high-stakes settlements.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A litigation-only firm can turn its narrow focus into a steady source of work. Full-service firms often have to decline disputes because an opposing party is already a client. A litigation boutique has fewer transactional relationships that create those conflicts, so it can take more of those cases. Full-service firms can also refer disputes to the boutique with little risk of losing the client’s corporate or transactional work.

The focus also lets the firm put its hiring, training, and technology behind one practice. Repeated courtroom experience can build a reputation that attracts high-stakes matters and supports premium rates. Where the firm has the capital and appetite for risk, contingency or hybrid fees can turn successful cases into substantial profits. The trade-off is greater exposure to uneven case flow and outcomes, while full-service firms can spread that risk across practices.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A litigation-only firm can often take cases that a full-service firm has to turn down. A full-service firm may be legally barred from suing a current corporate client, even over an unrelated matter. It may also hesitate to sue a bank that regularly sends it financing work. A litigation-only firm has fewer of those conflicts and business ties, so it can take either side of a dispute, including claims against major companies. It still has to check for conflicts in every case.

That independence can also generate referrals. A full-service firm can send a dispute it cannot handle to a litigation specialist with little risk of losing the client’s deal work. Meanwhile, the specialist concentrates its hiring, training, and reputation on winning disputes. For clients facing a high-stakes case, that combination of availability and focused experience can justify premium fees.
